column1: What is nanpa-linja-n?
column2:
A notation system that reversibly encodes decimal digit strings as proper names and numeric cartouches.

It does not add new words to the Toki Pona lexicon.

column1: How does every nanpa-linja-n numeric proper name begin and end?
column2:
It begins with Ne- and ends with -n.

Example: 125 → Newatulun.

column1: How are multi-digit values formed?
column2:
Concatenate one designated syllable for each decimal digit between initial Ne- and final -n.

Relaxed 125: Ne + wa + tu + lu + n → Newatulun.

column1: Where may a long numeric proper name be split into words?
column2:
At numeric punctuation markers.

The marker’s initial n normally closes the preceding word: 2.5 → Netun One Lun.

column1: What is the exception to the normal punctuation word-splitting rule?
column2:
The negative marker no.

It can attach to initial Ne- as Neno: −5 → Neno Lun.

column1: Which mode should beginners normally produce?
column2:
Relaxed mode.

Strict forms remain useful for recognition, but relaxed mode supplies the preferred output forms used in this deck.

column1: How are exact hundreds optionally split?
column2:
The final two zeros may be written as a separate Inin word.

100 → Newan Inin; 200 → Netun Inin.

column1: What changes when a numeric cartouche is abbreviated?
column2:
Interior supporting nena, en and open glyphs are removed where the specification permits.

The value and pronunciation remain the same. Optional spacer en glyphs may still be shown.
